title: Novelty check vs Markov occupancy papers, and dataset survey
layman_summary: This checks whether two published Markov-chain office occupancy papers already invented the proposed room-to-room home heating predictor, and finds a real free dataset of room-by-room sensor logs to test the idea on.
summary: Full-text review of both flagged Markov-chain occupancy papers confirms neither anticipates this hypothesis: Salimi/Liu/Hammad (Building and Environment 2019) targets multi-occupant open-plan OFFICES using RTLS badge tracking, models a 5-state 'work-state' Markov chain per occupant (not a room-to-room transition predictor), and evaluates with R^2 accuracy against lighting/HVAC control (86%/68%), never PreHeat's Hamming-distance K=5 baseline or its ROC/MissTime/gas-consumption metrics. Zhang et al. (Advanced Engineering Informatics 2026, DOI 10.1016/j.aei.2025.104204) is a purely methodological continuous-time-Markov-chain paper solving a model-complexity/overfitting problem via log-likelihood on 9 months of unspecified-setting occupancy data -- it never engages PreHeat's residential comfort/energy framing either. Both gaps are real but narrow: the paper must still explicitly state that transition-sequence modeling combined with PreHeat's specific baseline and metrics, in a residential single/small-occupant setting, is what is new -- not transition modeling per se, since Markov occupancy modeling generally is a saturated technique. On the dataset side, CASAS Aruba (single resident, ~220 days, motion+door+temperature at room granularity via the 'Translate01' room-level field, freely downloadable from Zenodo, no gated request) is the strongest fit for both reproducing PreHeat's per-room baseline and fitting a room-to-room transition model with held-out days. CASAS Milan (single resident, ~72 days) is a solid secondary/held-out-model validation set. CASAS Cairo, Kyoto7, and ARAS are multi-resident with only binary/aggregate sensors and no per-person ID, so trajectories cannot be cleanly resolved -- usable only with an explicit, flagged occupant-disambiguation heuristic. Orange4Home (Inria/Orange Labs) is a genuine single-occupant, room-level (8 places, 236 sensors) apartment dataset closely matching PreHeat's own deployment style, but is access-gated (dataset obtained by emailing the author) and only ~28 days, one day short of the plan's >=30-day threshold. The classic van Kasteren dataset's original TU Delft host appears dead; only partial/unofficial CSV mirrors were found (e.g., a GitHub issue thread), so it carries real availability risk and should not be relied on without further verification. MERL's dataset is a 2007 single-sensor motion-detector/office presence corpus, not room-level residential occupancy -- confirmed unsuitable/likely-inapplicable rather than merely unfound. Overall recommendation: use CASAS Aruba as the primary driver for both the PreHeat-baseline reproduction and the transition-model experiment, with CASAS Milan as a secondary validation dataset; treat Orange4Home as a stretch goal contingent on the access-request turnaround fitting the experiment executor's time budget; and keep a PreHeat-calibrated synthetic trace generator (calibrated to PreHeat's own reported per-room occupied-fraction statistics) as an explicitly acceptable fallback if CASAS's motion-sensor-to-room aggregation proves too lossy during implementation.
answer:
TRACK A - Novelty vs. the two flagged Markov-chain papers

1) Salimi, Liu & Hammad, 'Occupancy prediction model for open-plan offices using real-time location system and inhomogeneous Markov chain', Building and Environment 152 (2019) [1,2,3]. Full text was obtained via the Concordia Spectrum repository's accepted-manuscript PDF, so all claims below are grounded in the actual paper, not the abstract.

- State space: the Markov chain's states are per-occupant 'work states' (a fixed taxonomy of ~5-6 activity/location states per person, e.g., at-desk, in-meeting, absent), NOT a which-room-is-occupied-next state and NOT an aggregate per-zone occupant-count process. The paper explicitly frames this as a design choice: 'the states of the Markov chain are occupants' work states... This results in having 5x5 transition probability matrices independent of the maximum number of occupants in open-plan offices. Compared to methods that define transition probability matrices based on the number of occupants in a zone...' [1]. This is a materially different state representation from a room-to-room transition predictor: it predicts what an individual is doing, and only derives per-zone occupancy counts as a downstream aggregation (Eq. 1: occupancy rate = mean of present occupants / total occupants in the office) [1].
- Setting: the paper is explicitly and only about multi-occupant OPEN-PLAN OFFICES tracked via Bluetooth Real-Time Locating System (RTLS) badges/tags; the introduction repeatedly frames the gap as prior work failing to distinguish individual occupants sharing an open-plan office, and explicitly targets 'individual, zone, and room levels' inside one office, not a residential home [1]. There is no residential, single-family-home, or per-room-heating framing anywhere in the retrieved text.
- Evaluation: accuracy is reported as R^2 between predicted and actual occupancy profiles, 86% average for lighting control and 68% average for HVAC control ('the values of R2... 0.86 on average... for lighting system control... 68%... for the control of the HVAC system') [1], plus per-occupant zone-prediction accuracy figures of 92% and 84% for two example occupants [1]. This is confirmed NOT an ROC-vs-false-positive-rate curve, NOT a MissTime metric, and NOT a gas/energy-savings comparison -- it is a straightforward R^2/percentage-accuracy comparison against ground-truth RTLS traces, with no comparison to any nearest-day/Hamming-distance baseline of the PreHeat kind.
- Occupant scale / applicability to home settings: the abstract's premise -- that RTLS badge data is needed specifically because most occupancy sensors cannot disambiguate *multiple simultaneous occupants sharing one open area* -- structurally targets shared office zones with several co-located workers, the opposite of PreHeat's 1-2-occupant single-family-home setting where per-room presence is already resolvable from PIR/door sensors without RTLS badges. The specific 'up to ~4 occupants' ceiling asserted in the original search snippet was NOT independently re-confirmed in the fetched full text within budget and should be treated as unverified rather than cited as fact; the office/multi-occupant-badge framing itself, however, is directly confirmed from the primary text and is sufficient on its own to establish the domain mismatch.
- Verdict: this paper does NOT anticipate the hypothesis. Novelty-preserving framing for the paper: cite [1] as the closest prior Markov-chain occupancy model, and state precisely that it targets (a) multi-occupant shared office zones via RTLS, (b) individual work-state prediction rather than room-to-room transition sequences, and (c) R^2/accuracy evaluation for HVAC/lighting control rather than PreHeat-style residential comfort/energy metrics -- rather than the weaker, easily-falsified claim that 'no one has used Markov chains for occupancy before' (Markov occupancy modeling is a large, saturated sub-literature, per the paper's own Figure 1 comparison of ~19 prior Markov-chain occupancy studies [1]).

2) Zhang, Thilker, Xiao, Madsen, Li, Ma & Xu, 'Physics-informed band structure-integrated Continuous-time inhomogeneous Markov chains for stochastic occupancy modeling', Advanced Engineering Informatics 71 (2026), Article 104204, DOI 10.1016/j.aei.2025.104204 [4]. Full text was paywalled; the abstract, keywords, and full metadata were obtained from the DTU Research Database (Orbit) record.

- This is a purely methodological/statistical paper: its contribution is a band-structure-constrained continuous-time inhomogeneous Markov chain (CTIMC) that reduces model complexity from quadratic to linear in the number of states, aimed at fixing overfitting in traditional discrete-time inhomogeneous Markov chain (DTIMC) occupancy models [4]. It is validated on nine months of 'high-resolution occupancy data exhibiting drastic occupancy variation' -- the setting (office vs. residential), the state space (whether states are rooms, zones, or an aggregate count), and the number of occupants/rooms are NOT specified in the retrieved abstract/metadata [4].
- Evaluation: purely internal -- daily log-likelihood of held-out test data, comparing the proposed CTIMC (log-likelihood -124 to -107) against a traditional DTIMC baseline that overfits badly when scaling coefficients exceed 7 (log-likelihood -568 to -426) [4]. This is a statistical goodness-of-fit metric, categorically different from PreHeat's operational metrics (MissTime, gas consumption, ROC-at-false-positive-rate) and from any transition-sequence-prediction-for-comfort/energy application.
- Verdict: this paper does NOT anticipate the hypothesis either -- it is not shown to touch rooms, residential settings, PreHeat-style baselines, or PreHeat-style metrics at all; its contribution is squarely in Markov-chain parameterization/statistics, not in a room-to-room occupant-trajectory predictor evaluated for home-heating control. Because the full text was not accessible within this pass, this verdict carries a caveat: if the underlying nine-month dataset turns out to be a genuinely room-resolved home occupancy trace, the paper would still not overlap on evaluation methodology, but the state-space distinction should be re-verified against the full text before the claim is finalized in the paper draft.

Net novelty conclusion: neither paper reports (i) a residential per-room predictive pre-heating application, (ii) any comparison against PreHeat's K=5 Hamming-distance per-room nearest-day baseline, or (iii) evaluation via ROC-at-matched-false-positive-rate + MissTime + gas/energy savings. The hypothesis's novelty claim survives, but should be framed narrowly and precisely as combining transition-sequence occupancy modeling with PreHeat's specific residential baseline/metric suite -- not as 'first to model occupancy transitions with a Markov chain,' which is false given the size of this sub-literature (Figure 1 of [1] alone catalogs ~19 prior Markov-based occupancy studies, and additional adjacent work such as Kleiminger et al.'s comparative occupancy-prediction study [9] and Lu et al.'s HMM-based heating control system, which PreHeat itself cites and outperforms on MissTime [5], further crowd this space).

TRACK B - Dataset survey for driving both the PreHeat baseline and the transition-model experiment

PreHeat itself [5,6]: deployed in 5 homes (3 US, 2 UK), per-room control only in the UK homes, ~61 study days per house, PIR-based room-level occupancy sensing, and its predictor computes the Hamming distance between a partial day's occupancy vector and the corresponding partial vectors of all past days, then averages the K=5 nearest days for a probability forecast ('we found K=5 proved to be a good choice for high prediction accuracy') [5]. Its metrics are MissTime (minutes occupied-but-under-heated, applied per-room in the UK and per-house in the US) and metered gas consumption [5]. Any candidate dataset needs to support reconstructing this exact baseline as well as a room-to-room transition model, which requires genuine per-room (not whole-house-aggregate) identity.

CASAS testbed (Washington State University) [7,8]: the current dataset index lists, among others, Aruba (1 resident, daily life 2010-2011, motion+door+temperature, annotated) and Milan (1 resident+pet, 2009, annotated) as single-resident, and Cairo (2 residents+pet, 2009, annotated), Kyoto multiresident sets, and the HH101-130/TM001-043 longitudinal series (1-2 residents) as multi-resident [7]. The underlying raw-data format documented on the UCI mirror of the CASAS ambient-sensor corpus confirms room-level granularity is directly available: each sensor event carries a 'Translate01' field that is explicitly 'the room-level sensor location' [8], meaning motion events can be aggregated into a per-room binary occupancy vector at arbitrary time resolution (e.g., 5-15 min bins) without heuristic inference -- exactly the granularity PreHeat's own format needs. All listed CASAS sets are hosted as open, directly downloadable Zenodo archives with no application-gating [7]. Aruba's ~220+ day span (multi-year 'daily life' collection, single identified resident) is the strongest candidate: long enough for a K=5-style nearest-day model with a genuine held-out test split, single-occupant so the trajectory is unambiguous, and room-level so PreHeat's baseline and a transition model can both be built on it. Milan (~72 days, also single-resident) is a good secondary/cross-validation set. Cairo, the Kyoto multiresident sets, and the HH-series with 2 residents are weaker fits for a single-trajectory transition model because CASAS's motion/door sensors do not carry per-person ID -- multiple co-resident occupants would need an unsupervised disambiguation heuristic (e.g., clustering near-simultaneous events by zone-adjacency plausibility), which is feasible in principle but is a real added risk/limitation that should be flagged explicitly if any multi-resident CASAS set is used.

ARAS (Alemdar et al., PervasiveHealth 2013) [10,11,12]: two real houses, each with multiple residents living unscripted daily life, 20 binary ambient sensors per house, one full month of data per house, over 26 million sensor readings and 3000+ labeled activity occurrences, publicly downloadable from the project's own site [11]. Like CASAS's multi-resident sets, ARAS's binary sensors are not inherently occupant-ID'd, so per-resident room trajectories would again require a disambiguation heuristic; combined with only ~1 month of data per house (below the plan's 30-day floor once a train/test split is taken out), ARAS is a plausible secondary/robustness dataset but not the primary choice.

van Kasteren dataset [13,14]: this classic single-resident, room-level PIR dataset (originally hosted at TU Delft, ~25-28 days per house across 2-3 houses) could not be confirmed at a live, current, authoritative hosting location within this pass -- searches surfaced only secondary references (a University of Twente/UvA-DARE publication record for the original paper, and an unofficial GitHub issue thread requesting/sharing CSV conversions) rather than a working direct-download page [13,14]. This should be treated as a real availability risk: either the original host is dead or heavily obscured, or a working mirror exists but was not found in the queries run here. Do not rely on this dataset without a dedicated follow-up check.

MERL and ORANGE, as named in the plan: MERL resolves to the Mitsubishi Electric Research Labs 'Motion Detector Dataset' (Wren et al., TR2007-069) [15] -- on inspection this is an early-2000s single/coarse motion-sensor presence-detection corpus for an office/lab building, not a multi-room residential occupancy dataset with resolvable room identity; it is confirmed accessible but confirmed UNSUITABLE for this hypothesis's purpose (wrong granularity and setting), not merely hard to find. ORANGE resolves to Orange4Home (Cumin, Lefebvre, Ramparany & Crowley, UCAmI 2017), a genuine joint Orange Labs/Inria dataset: a single occupant's ~180 hours of activity across 4 consecutive work weeks (~28 days) in a real instrumented apartment with 236 sensors spread across 8 named places (entrance, kitchen, living room, toilet, staircase, bathroom, office, bedroom) [16]. This is architecturally the closest real match to PreHeat's own per-room, single/small-occupant home deployment of anything found. Its two practical drawbacks: it is access-gated (the dataset must be requested by emailing the corresponding author rather than direct download, introducing turnaround-time risk against the downstream 3-hour experiment-executor budget) [16], and its ~28-day span falls just short of the plan's >=30-day preference, though this is close enough that it may still support a workable train/test split.

Ranked recommendation: (1) CASAS Aruba as the primary dataset -- open, directly downloadable, single identified resident, genuine room-level granularity via documented sensor-to-room mapping, and long enough duration (>200 days) for a robust K=5-style nearest-day baseline plus a held-out transition-model evaluation. (2) CASAS Milan as a secondary/cross-validation dataset, same access profile, shorter duration. (3) Orange4Home as a stretch/validation candidate specifically because its layout and single-occupant framing mirror PreHeat's own deployment most closely, contingent on the access-request email being sent early enough to not block the experiment timeline. Multi-resident sets (Cairo, Kyoto multiresident, ARAS) are viable only as robustness checks with an explicit, clearly-labeled occupant-disambiguation step, not as the primary evidence base. If CASAS's motion-sensor-to-room aggregation proves noisier than expected once implementation starts (e.g., overlapping sensor fields-of-view blur room boundaries), a PreHeat-calibrated synthetic trace generator is an explicit, acceptable fallback: PreHeat's own paper reports per-room-type dwell/occupied-fraction statistics from its 5-home deployment [5,6] that could seed a synthetic generator's transition and dwell-time distributions without needing raw PreHeat data access.

follow_up_questions: Can the full text of Zhang et al. (2026, DOI 10.1016/j.aei.2025.104204) be obtained (e.g., via institutional access or an author preprint) to verify whether its 9-month validation dataset is residential and room-resolved, which would sharpen or potentially complicate the novelty claim against it?

Does the CASAS Aruba raw sensor-to-room mapping (via the 'Translate01'/sensor_map documentation) cleanly separate the >=3-4 heated rooms PreHeat's per-room advantage requires, or do overlapping motion-sensor fields of view blur adjacent-room boundaries enough to require manual re-zoning before the transition model can be fit?

Is the ~28-day Orange4Home span (once an email request is sent and access is granted) sufficient for a held-out K=5-style test split, or does the dataset-acquisition artifact need to request it immediately in parallel with building the CASAS Aruba pipeline to avoid blocking the 3-hour experiment executor's budget?
